Fruit and vegetable intake and the risk of cardiovascular disease, total cancer and all-cause mortality—a systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. International Journal of Epidemiology, 46(3), 1029–1056. https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw319

Nourish.text: Include legumes (beans, lentils, chickpeas) or whole grains (e.g., oats, brown rice, quinoa) in at least 3 meals this week.
Nourish.why: This practice broadens a single "eat healthier" instinct into a concrete, repeatable checklist — offering two flexible ingredient categories across several meals lowers decision fatigue compared with a single rigid rule.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that higher whole grain intake is associated with reduced risk of coronary heart disease, cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all-cause mortality in a dose-dependent manner, with benefits observed up to roughly seven servings/day.Scientific rationale (legumes): Evidence suggests that higher legume intake is associated with reduced risk of ischemic heart disease specifically; the same analysis did not find a significant association between legume intake and stroke or diabetes risk.
references: Afshin, A., Micha, R., Khatibzadeh, S., & Mozaffarian, D. (2014). Consumption of nuts and legumes and risk of incident ischemic heart disease, stroke, and diabetes: A systematic review and meta-analysis. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 100(1), 278–288. https://doi.org/10.3945/ajcn.113.076901. Aune, D., Keum, N., Giovannucci, E., Fadnes, L. T., Boffetta, P., Greenwood, D. C., Tonstad, S., Vatten, L. J., Riboli, E., & Norat, T. (2016). Whole grain consumption and risk of cardiovascular disease, cancer, and all cause and cause specific mortality: Systematic review and dose-response meta-analysis of prospective studies. BMJ, 353, Article i2716. https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.i2716

Nourish.text: Include a palm-sized serving of protein at all three main meals on at least 3 days this week.
Nourish.why: This progression moves participants from a simple inclusion habit (add protein) to a portioned, repeatable routine (palm-sized serving, multiple days), and finally to advance planning that removes in-the-moment decisions entirely, reducing the daily willpower required to eat consistently well.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that dietary protein supplementation significantly increases gains in strength, fat-free mass, and muscle fibre size during resistance training lasting six weeks or longer, with the benefit diminishing above a total protein intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day.
references: Morton, R. W. et al. (2018). Systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength.

Halton, T. L., & Hu, F. B. (2004). The effects of high protein diets on thermogenesis, satiety and weight loss: A critical review. Journal of the American College of Nutrition, 23(5), 373–385. https://doi.org/10.1080/07315724.2004.10719381

Nourish.text: This week, count how many different plant foods you eat (fruit, vegetables, beans, whole grains, nuts, seeds and herbs all count). If your number is under 10, try adding one or two new ones — this is a good first step toward greater variety.
Nourish.why: This practice uses a personal count as a low-stakes self-monitoring tool, building awareness of current variety without presenting an arbitrary number as an evidenced target, and can scaffold toward a higher-variety goal at a later stage.
Nourish.evidence: Evidence suggests that people who consume more than 30 different plant types per week have greater gut microbiome diversity — including higher abundance of certain short-chain-fatty-acid-producing bacteria — than those who consume 10 or fewer plant types per week.  Research also indicates that higher-protein meals increase diet-induced thermogenesis and satiety, and tend to reduce subsequent energy intake, compared to lower-protein meals of equivalent calories — though the review's own authors note that findings on whether this reliably translates into greater weight or fat loss have been inconsistent.
references: McDonald, D., Hyde, E., Debelius, J. W., Morton, J. T., Gonzalez, A., Ackermann, G., Aksenov, A. A., Behsaz, B., Brennan, C., Chen, Y., DeRight Goldasich, L., Dorrestein, P. C., Dunn, R. R., Fahimipour, A. K., Gaffney, J., Gilbert, J. A., Gogul, G., Green, J. L., Hugenholtz, P., . . . Knight, R. (2018). American Gut: An open platform for citizen science microbiome research. mSystems, 3(3), Article e00031-18. https://doi.org/10.1128/mSystems.00031-18

Nourish.text: Plan five weekday lunches and dinners in advance, making protein the starting point for every meal before adding vegetables, fibre-rich carbohydrates and healthy fats.
Nourish.why: This practice removes in-the-moment meal decisions entirely by shifting planning to a single weekly session, and establishing protein as the fixed starting point for every meal gives participants one consistent anchor to build the rest of the plate around, reducing the cognitive load of five separate daily choices.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that dietary protein supplementation significantly increases gains in strength, fat-free mass, and muscle fibre size during resistance training lasting six weeks or longer, with the benefit diminishing above a total protein intake of about 1.6 g/kg/day.
references: Morton, R. W. et al. (2018). Systematic review, meta-analysis and meta-regression of the effect of protein supplementation on resistance training-induced gains in muscle mass and strength.

Halton, T. L., & Hu, F. B. (2004). The effects of high protein diets on thermogenesis, satiety and weight loss: A critical review. Journal of the American College of Nutrition, 23(5), 373–385. https://doi.org/10.1080/07315724.2004.10719381

Nourish.text: Cook at least one meal from minimally processed ingredients every day this week.
Nourish.why: This practice creates a small, repeatable daily commitment — one meal, not the whole day — making the habit achievable within a busy week while establishing a minimally-processed cooking routine that can expand over time.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that, under controlled conditions, an ultra-processed diet led participants to eat roughly 500 more calories per day and gain weight over two weeks, compared to an unprocessed diet matched for calories, macronutrients, sugar, sodium, and fibre.
references: Hall, K. D. et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain. Cell Metabolism. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008

Nourish.text: For one week, compare ingredient lists before buying packaged foods and choose the option with the fewest recognisable ingredients whenever possible.
Nourish.why: This practice moves control upstream to the shopping environment rather than the meal itself, building a durable decision-making rule that reduces reliance on willpower or in-the-moment choices.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that, compared to a matched unprocessed diet, an ultra-processed diet led to significantly higher energy intake and weight gain in a controlled setting.
references: Hall, K. D. et al. (2019). Ultra-processed diets cause excess calorie intake and weight gain. Cell Metabolism. https://doi.org/10.1016/j.cmet.2019.05.008

Nourish.text: Drink a glass of water before every main meal for the entire week and note any changes in your hunger or fullness.
Nourish.why: This progression adds self-monitoring — noticing hunger and fullness — turning a simple mechanical habit into a source of personal feedback, reinforcing the behavior through the participant's own observed experience rather than instruction alone.
Nourish.evidence: Research indicates that drinking a 568 ml glass of water immediately before a meal reduces energy intake at that meal and increases self-reported fullness and satisfaction, compared to eating without a water preload.  Research also indicates that among overweight/obese adults aged 55–75 following a calorie-restricted diet, those who drank 500 ml of water before each meal lost significantly more weight over 12 weeks than those on the same diet without the water routine.
references: Corney, R. A., Sunderland, C., & James, L. J. (2016). Immediate pre-meal water ingestion decreases voluntary food intake in lean young males. European Journal of Nutrition, 55(2), 815–819. https://doi.org/10.1007/s00394-015-0903-4

Dennis, E. A., Dengo, A. L., Comber, D. L., Flack, K. D., Savla, J., Davy, K. P., & Davy, B. M. (2010). Water consumption increases weight loss during a hypocaloric diet intervention in middle-aged and older adults. Obesity, 18(2), 300–307. https://doi.org/10.1038/oby.2009.235

Rhythm.text: Eat breakfast (or first meal) at a consistent time.
Rhythm.why: This practice targets the single most predictable meal of the day as an entry point, giving participants an easy first win before asking them to coordinate multiple meal times.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that following an irregular meal pattern, compared to a regular one, produces higher insulin responses to food and higher fasting cholesterol, even when total daily calorie intake is unchanged.
references: Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077.

Rhythm.text: Eat your main meals at roughly the same times each day, and avoid eating or drinking anything except water within 2 hours of going to bed.
Rhythm.why: This practice combines two related habits — regular timing and a clear bedtime cutoff — into one simple rule, reducing the number of separate decisions needed each evening.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that following an irregular meal pattern produces worse insulin and cholesterol markers than a regular one. Separately, evidence from a nationally representative time-use survey found that eating or drinking within an hour of bedtime was associated with more fragmented sleep, though also with longer total sleep duration.
references: Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077. Iao, S. I., Jansen, E., Shedden, K., et al. (2022). Associations between bedtime eating or drinking, sleep duration and wake after sleep onset: findings from the American Time Use Survey. British Journal of Nutrition, 127(12), 1888–1897.

Rhythm.text: Keep a consistent daily eating schedule by having your first and last meal at roughly the same times each day.
Rhythm.why: This progression extends a single-meal habit (breakfast) to anchor both ends of the day, giving participants a broader but still simple structural rule.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that an irregular meal pattern produces higher insulin responses and worse fasting cholesterol than a regular one. Separately, evidence from a controlled laboratory study indicates that shifting meal timing later can delay the body's glucose rhythms and shift clock-gene expression in adipose tissue.
references: Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077..Wehrens, S. M. T., et al. (2017). Meal Timing Regulates the Human Circadian System. Current Biology, 27(12), 1768–1775.e3.

Rhythm.text: Aim for three structured meals today instead of grazing throughout the day.
Rhythm.why: This practice interrupts habitual grazing by giving participants a concrete structure (three defined meals) to plan around, rather than relying on willpower to resist snacking in the moment.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that an irregular, higher-frequency eating pattern (3–9 occasions per day) produces worse insulin and cholesterol markers than a fixed, structured pattern.
references: Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077.

Rhythm.text: Eat lunch within the same one-hour window on at least 5 days this week.
Rhythm.why: This practice targets the meal most people can control most easily during a workday, using a fixed window to build predictability without requiring exact minute-by-minute timing.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that, among people in a structured weight-loss program, those who ate their main midday meal later lost significantly less weight over 20 weeks than those who ate earlier, despite similar calorie intake and sleep duration.
references: Garaulet, M., Gómez-Abellán, P., Alburquerque-Béjar, J. J., et al. (2013). Timing of food intake predicts weight loss effectiveness. International Journal of Obesity, 37(4), 604–611.Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077.

Rhythm.text: Finish dinner within the same one-hour window on at least 5 days this week.
Rhythm.why: This practice isolates the meal most likely to drift later in the evening and gives it its own fixed target, since dinner timing is often the least structured meal of the day.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that shifting the timing of the evening meal later, as part of a delayed daily meal schedule, delays the body's glucose rhythms and shifts clock-gene expression in fat tissue, even when total sleep is unaffected.
references: Wehrens, S. M. T., et al. (2017). Meal Timing Regulates the Human Circadian System. Current Biology, 27(12), 1768–1775.e3.Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077.

Rhythm.text: Choose a 10–12 hour daily eating window and keep your first and last meal within that window on at least 5 days this week.
Rhythm.why: This practice sets an outer boundary rather than a rigid schedule, giving participants flexibility in exactly when they eat while still creating a clear daily fasting period.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that overweight adults with an eating window wider than 14 hours who compressed their intake to 10–11 hours daily for 16 weeks reduced body weight and reported improved energy and sleep, with benefits maintained at one year. A separate single-arm trial in patients with diagnosed metabolic syndrome found that a 10-hour eating window improved weight, blood pressure, and lipid markers over 12 weeks.
references: Gill, S., & Panda, S. (2015). A Smartphone App Reveals Erratic Diurnal Eating Patterns in Humans that Can Be Modulated for Health Benefits. Cell Metabolism, 22(5), 789–798.Wilkinson, M. J., Manoogian, E. N. C., Zadourian, A., et al. (2020). Ten-Hour Time-Restricted Eating Reduces Weight, Blood Pressure, and Atherogenic Lipids in Patients with Metabolic Syndrome. Cell Metabolism, 31(1), 92–104.e5.

Rhythm.text: Finish your last calorie-containing food at least 3 hours before your usual bedtime everyday.
Rhythm.why: This practice gives participants a specific, checkable cutoff rather than a vague instruction to "eat earlier," making the habit easier to self-monitor.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that, in a nationally representative time-use survey, a shorter gap between eating and bedtime was associated with increased sleep fragmentation, with this association weakening as the gap widened toward three hours.
references: Iao, S. I., Jansen, E., Shedden, K., et al. (2022). Associations between bedtime eating or drinking, sleep duration and wake after sleep onset: findings from the American Time Use Survey. British Journal of Nutrition, 127(12), 1888–1897.

Rhythm.text: Before the week begins, choose approximate times for breakfast, lunch and dinner for your workdays and follow that schedule on at least 5 days this week.
Rhythm.why: This practice moves the planning decision to before the week starts, removing in-the-moment timing decisions and turning the consistency principle from Practices 1 and 3 into a deliberate, pre-committed routine.
Rhythm.evidence: Research indicates that an irregular meal pattern produces higher insulin responses and worse fasting cholesterol than a regular one. Separately, evidence from a controlled laboratory study indicates that shifting meal timing later can delay the body's glucose rhythms and shift clock-gene expression in adipose tissue.
references: Farshchi, H. R., Taylor, M. A., & Macdonald, I. A. (2004). Regular meal frequency creates more appropriate insulin sensitivity and lipid profiles compared with irregular meal frequency in healthy lean women. European Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 58(7), 1071–1077.Wehrens, S. M. T., et al. (2017). Meal Timing Regulates the Human Circadian System. Current Biology, 27(12), 1768–1775.e3.

Presence.text: Eat one main meal today without your phone, TV or computer.
Presence.why: This practice targets a single, clearly bounded meal, giving participants a low-effort way to test the habit before extending it further.
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that eating while distracted by television specifically increases how much people eat during that meal, and eating while distracted by any means increases how much people eat at their next eating occasion afterward.
references: Gough, T., Mann, T., Ahmadyar, K., Finlay, I., Jones, A., Tapper, K., & Robinson, E. (2026). Eating while distracted: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of distraction on concurrent and later energy intake in adults. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 123(6), 101315.Robinson, E., Aveyard, P., Daley, A., Jolly, K., Lewis, A., Lycett, D., & Higgs, S. (2013). Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 97(4), 728–742.

Presence.text: Before your first bite, take one slow breath to pause and bring your attention to the meal.
Presence.why: This practice uses a single physical action (one slow breath) as a trigger to transition attention toward the meal, giving participants a concrete, repeatable cue rather than an abstract instruction to "be present."
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that a brief mindfulness instruction delivered immediately before eating increases enjoyment of the food, and in one experiment, this same brief instruction led to eating less of an unhealthy food, with the reduction in intake explained by the increase in enjoyment.
references: Arch, J. J., Brown, K. W., Goodman, R. J., Della Porta, M. D., Kiken, L. G., & Tillman, S. (2016). Enjoying food without caloric cost: The impact of brief mindfulness on laboratory eating outcomes. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 79, 23–34.

Presence.text: Put your fork down between a few bites and notice the taste before taking the next one.
Presence.why: This practice introduces a physical action (putting the fork down) as a concrete trigger for pacing, rather than relying on an abstract instruction to "eat slower."
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that a slower eating rate is associated with lower energy intake compared to a faster eating rate, based on a meta-analysis of 22 experimental studies.
references: Robinson, E., Almiron-Roig, E., Rutters, F., de Graaf, C., Forde, C. G., Tudur Smith, C., Nolan, S. J., & Jebb, S. A. (2014). A systematic review and meta-analysis examining the effect of eating rate on energy intake and hunger. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 100(1), 123–151.

Presence.text: During one meal today, pause and notice one flavour, texture or smell you haven't paid attention to before.
Presence.why: This practice narrows the instruction to noticing just one previously unattended sensory detail, making the exercise achievable in a single meal rather than asking for sustained attention throughout.
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that instructing people to attend to the sensory properties of food while eating increases how much they enjoy it, and this enjoyment effect held even for a food with mixed or neutral associations, not just an inherently pleasurable one.
references: Arch, J. J., Brown, K. W., Goodman, R. J., Della Porta, M. D., Kiken, L. G., & Tillman, S. (2016). Enjoying food without caloric cost: The impact of brief mindfulness on laboratory eating outcomes. Behaviour Research and Therapy, 79, 23–34.

Presence.text: Eat every dinner this week without your phone, TV or computer.
Presence.why: This progression extends a single-meal habit to one meal type every day, building consistency around the meal most commonly eaten in front of a screen.
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that eating while distracted by television specifically increases how much people eat during that meal, and eating while distracted by any means increases how much people eat at their next eating occasion afterward.
references: Gough, T., Mann, T., Ahmadyar, K., Finlay, I., Jones, A., Tapper, K., & Robinson, E. (2026). Eating while distracted: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of distraction on concurrent and later energy intake in adults. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 123(6), 101315.Robinson, E., Aveyard, P., Daley, A., Jolly, K., Lewis, A., Lycett, D., & Higgs, S. (2013). Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 97(4), 728–742.

Presence.text: For the first five minutes of each meal, eat without multitasking and pay attention to the taste, texture and smell of your food.
Presence.why: This practice creates a bounded, low-effort window (five minutes) rather than asking for sustained attention throughout an entire meal, making the habit easier to start and maintain.
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that eating while distracted increases food intake at that meal and especially at the next eating occasion; separately, evidence on enhancing awareness of food during eating has not shown a significant effect on how much is eaten in the same sitting.
references: Gough, T., Mann, T., Ahmadyar, K., Finlay, I., Jones, A., Tapper, K., & Robinson, E. (2026). Eating while distracted: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of distraction on concurrent and later energy intake in adults. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 123(6), 101315.Robinson, E., Aveyard, P., Daley, A., Jolly, K., Lewis, A., Lycett, D., & Higgs, S. (2013). Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 97(4), 728–742.

Presence.text: Eat all main meals this week without your phone, TV or computer.
Presence.why: This progression extends the habit to its most demanding version, covering all main meals across the week, building on the smaller wins established at Gentle and Moderate levels.
Presence.evidence: Research indicates that eating while distracted by television specifically increases how much people eat during that meal, and eating while distracted by any means increases how much people eat at their next eating occasion afterward.
references: Gough, T., Mann, T., Ahmadyar, K., Finlay, I., Jones, A., Tapper, K., & Robinson, E. (2026). Eating while distracted: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of distraction on concurrent and later energy intake in adults. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 123(6), 101315.Robinson, E., Aveyard, P., Daley, A., Jolly, K., Lewis, A., Lycett, D., & Higgs, S. (2013). Eating attentively: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of food intake memory and awareness on eating. American Journal of Clinical Nutrition, 97(4), 728–742.

Share.text: Share one meal this week with a friend, family member or colleague.
Share.why: This practice sets the lowest possible bar, one meal, to establish a new social habit before asking participants to coordinate anything more demanding.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that people who eat socially with others more often report greater happiness, life satisfaction, trust, and community engagement, with a path analysis suggesting eating together drives these feelings rather than the reverse.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: Share one healthy recipe with someone in your Circle, and cook it together or eat it at the same time this week.
Share.why: This practice uses the natural influence of visible peer choices, making a new healthy option feel like an unremarkable, low-risk thing to try rather than a personal experiment.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that information about what other people are eating influences both how much food people eat and which specific foods they choose, with people significantly more likely to select a food after learning that others had chosen it.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.Robinson, E., Thomas, J., Aveyard, P., & Higgs, S. (2014). What everyone else is eating: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of informational eating norms on eating behavior. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 114(3), 414–429.

Share.text: Send one invitation this week to meet someone for coffee, lunch or dinner.
Share.why: This practice directly targets the specific gap the research identifies, between wanting to reach out and actually doing it, by asking for the one concrete action rather than relying on intention alone.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that most people who have lost touch with a friend want to reconnect but rarely act on it, even when they have the person's contact information, believe the person would appreciate hearing from them, and are given time to send a message.
references: Aknin, L. B., & Sandstrom, G. M. (2024). People are surprisingly hesitant to reach out to old friends. Communications Psychology, 2(1), 34.

Share.text: Invite someone to lunch or dinner and share the meal together this week.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that people who eat socially with others more often report greater happiness, life satisfaction, trust, and community engagement, with a path analysis suggesting eating together drives these feelings rather than the reverse.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: Cook one recipe shared by your Circle and tell them how it turned out.
Share.why: This practice builds a small feedback loop into an already-social action, prompting participants to close the loop with a message of thanks or appreciation, which research suggests strengthens a relationship more than the original gesture alone.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that when people perceive a gesture from someone as reflecting genuine responsiveness, they feel grateful, and that gratitude expressed during everyday interactions predicts improved relationship outcomes over the following month.
references: Algoe, S. B., Haidt, J., & Gable, S. L. (2008). Beyond reciprocity: gratitude and relationships in everyday life. Emotion, 8(3), 425–429.Robinson, E., Thomas, J., Aveyard, P., & Higgs, S. (2014). What everyone else is eating: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of informational eating norms on eating behavior. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 114(3), 414–429.

Share.text: Ask someone in your Circle to help you prepare one meal this week.
Share.why: This practice reframes meal preparation as collaborative rather than solitary, creating a natural, low-pressure opening to ask for help.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that people who eat socially with others more frequently report having more friends they can depend on for support.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: During one shared meal this week, share a memory or story from the past, or bring up something that made you laugh recently, with the people you're eating with.
Share.why: This practice gives participants two concrete, low-effort conversational moves, telling a story or bringing up something funny, rather than asking them to generate open-ended depth on the spot.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that shared meals involving more laughter and reminiscing are associated with greater feelings of closeness between those present.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: Host one shared meal this month and invite your Circle to contribute a dish or recipe.
Share.why: Distributing the effort, asking others to contribute a dish, lowers the logistical burden of hosting on any one person.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that shared meals involving more people are associated with greater feelings of closeness among those present.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., & Layton, J. B. (2010). Social Relationships and Mortality Risk: A Meta-analytic Review. PLoS Medicine, 7(7), e1000316.
Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: Invite someone who might otherwise eat alone to join you for a meal or coffee this week.
Share.why: This practice directs the shared-meal habit outward, toward someone else's isolation, reframing the behaviour as an act of inclusion rather than personal socializing.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that social isolation, loneliness, and living alone are each independently associated with a 26–32% increased risk of mortality, a magnitude comparable to other well-established risk factors.
references: Holt-Lunstad, J., Smith, T. B., Baker, M., Harris, T., & Stephenson, D. (2015). Loneliness and social isolation as risk factors for mortality: a meta-analytic review. Perspectives on Psychological Science, 10(2), 227–237. Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Share.text: After your shared meal, share one thing you learned or appreciated with your Circle.
Share.why: This practice adds a brief, structured moment of reflection right after the shared meal, converting the experience into an explicit expression of appreciation rather than letting it pass unacknowledged.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that expressing gratitude within an existing relationship, when perceived as sincere, predicts improvements in relationship quality over the following weeks.
references: Algoe, S. B., Haidt, J., & Gable, S. L. (2008). Beyond reciprocity: gratitude and relationships in everyday life. Emotion, 8(3), 425–429.Robinson, E., Thomas, J., Aveyard, P., & Higgs, S. (2014). What everyone else is eating: a systematic review and meta-analysis of the effect of informational eating norms on eating behavior. Journal of the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics, 114(3), 414–429.

Share.text: During one shared meal this week, invite everyone at the table to share a favourite memory or a story that still makes them laugh.
Share.why: This practice turns the Moderate-level individual habit into a group activity, distributing the conversational effort across everyone at the table rather than placing it on one person to ask a question.
Share.evidence: Research indicates that shared meals involving more laughter and reminiscing are associated with greater feelings of closeness between those present.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Celebrate.text: Cook a family recipe with a younger generation.
Celebrate.why: This practice pairs a shared cooking activity with intergenerational transmission, turning an ordinary task into a moment of passing on family identity and tradition.
Celebrate.evidence: Research indicates that people who eat socially with others more often report greater happiness, trust, and social support. Separately, a review of the family-rituals literature found that recurring family practices are associated with better parenting competence, child adjustment, and family relationship quality.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. Fiese, B. H., Tomcho, T. J., Douglas, M., Josephs, K., Poltrock, S., & Baker, T. (2002). A review of 50 years of research on naturally occurring family routines and rituals: cause for celebration? Journal of Family Psychology, 16(4), 381–390.

Celebrate.text: Share a memory about a meal or recipe that has special meaning to you.
Celebrate.why: This practice gives participants a specific type of content, a food memory, to bring into conversation, translating a research-identified correlate of closeness into a concrete, repeatable action.
Celebrate.evidence: Research indicates that shared meals involving more reminiscing about the past are associated with greater feelings of closeness among the people present.
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211.

Celebrate.text: Create one meal this week that feels worth celebrating, even if there's no special occasion.
Celebrate.why: This practice creates permission to elevate an ordinary meal without needing external justification, using ritual and intention, rather than an unusual occasion, as the mechanism for making a meal feel special.
Celebrate.evidence: Research indicates that performing a small ritual before eating increases how much people enjoy and value the food, compared with eating the same food without a ritual, with this effect holding even for ordinary foods.
references: Vohs, K. D., Wang, Y., Gino, F., & Norton, M. I. (2013). Rituals enhance consumption. Psychological Science, 24(9), 1714–1721.

Celebrate.text: Invite someone who hasn't shared a meal with you before to join you for lunch or dinner.
Celebrate.why: Research indicates that daily interactions with more peripheral or less familiar members of a person's social network are associated with greater daily happiness and a stronger sense of belonging. Separately, evidence on social eating indicates that shared meals are associated with feelings of trust and closeness with those present.
Celebrate.evidence: This practice deliberately targets a newer or less familiar connection rather than an existing close relationship, extending the shared-meal habit toward the kind of weak-tie interaction research suggests people undervalue.  Specifically validates that connecting with less-familiar people, not just close ties, contributes to wellbeing — a precise match for "hasn't shared a meal with you before."
references: Dunbar, R. I. M. (2017). Breaking bread: the functions of social eating. Adaptive Human Behavior and Physiology, 3(3), 198–211. Sandstrom, G. M., & Dunn, E. W. (2014). Social interactions and well-being: the surprising power of weak ties. Personality and Social Psychology Bulletin, 40(7), 910–922.

Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.why: This practice establishes a manageable daily target that builds early confidence and consistency before increasing the dose.
Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.evidence: Research indicates that daily step count is associated with progressively lower all-cause mortality risk, with meaningful reductions already evident at step counts below the study's identified plateau range of 8,000–10,000 steps per day.
references: Paluch, A. E., Bajpai, S., Bassett, D. R., Carnethon, M. R., Ekelund, U., Evenson, K. R., Galuska, D. A., Jefferis, B. J., Kraus, W. E., Lee, I. M., Matthews, C. E., Omura, J. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. The Lancet. Public health, 7(3), e219–e228. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9

Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.why: This progression raises the target toward the range associated with the greatest evidenced benefit, reinforcing the habit through repetition before it becomes an unconscious daily pattern.
Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.evidence: Research indicates that daily step count is associated with progressively lower all-cause mortality risk up to approximately 8,000–10,000 steps per day, the range where the largest cohort-wide risk reduction is observed.
references: Paluch, A. E., Bajpai, S., Bassett, D. R., Carnethon, M. R., Ekelund, U., Evenson, K. R., Galuska, D. A., Jefferis, B. J., Kraus, W. E., Lee, I. M., Matthews, C. E., Omura, J. Daily steps and all-cause mortality: a meta-analysis of 15 international cohorts. The Lancet. Public health, 7(3), e219–e228. https://doi.org/10.1016/S2468-2667(21)00302-9

Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.why: This progression shifts the focus at the Deep level from increasing volume to sustaining it — hitting the evidence-supported target consistently across most days of the week, rather than chasing a higher number the research doesn't support.
Incidental Movement & Sedentary Behavior.evidence: Research indicates that daily step count is associated with progressively lower all-cause mortality risk up to approximately 8,000–10,000 steps per day, after which additional steps show no further measurable reduction in risk.
